Date: 2026-03-27

Attendees: Maya Chen, Luis Ortega, Priya Kapoor (Redwood); Samir Patel, Julia Nguyen, Ravi Menon, Emma Torres (Atlas Payments)
summary: Technical deep dive on multi-region routing, failover policies, KV cache warmup/consistency, batching and quantization fallbacks for Atlas Payments. Covered policy routing (latency-first vs cost-first), regional capacity thresholds, sticky sessions, pre-warming KV cache, rollout playbooks, and security considerations for VPC/private deployments. Agreed action items: benchmark run, share docs, schedule install walkthrough.
topics: Routing policies; regional capacity and autoscale; DR playbook and runbooks; KV cache priming and consistency; batching strategies and impact on p95; quantized model fallbacks and quality regression checks; VPC/KMS/secure audit trails; on-prem warmstart considerations
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining on time, uh quick roll call please
[00:06] Samir Patel: Samir here, CTO Atlas
[00:08] Julia Nguyen: Julia, platform lead
[00:10] Ravi Menon: Ravi, security
[00:12] Emma Torres: Emma, SRE
[00:14] Luis Ortega: Luis from Redwood SE, hi all
[00:16] Maya Chen: great, so we wanted to walk through multi-region routing architecture and a pragmatic DR playbook, also talk about cache warmup and quantized fallbacks, sound good?
[00:25] Julia Nguyen: yes, especially the part about quantized fallbacks — we need to know quality delta and how to test it
[00:30] Luis Ortega: absolutely, we'll surface the numbers. quick context question: what are your p95 targets and typical burst shapes?
[00:36] Julia Nguyen: target p95 is 120 to 200ms depending on endpoint, but bursty payment batch jobs can spike to 6k rps for short windows, we usually expect traffic from US-East and EU-West primarily
[00:46] Samir Patel: and we have strict data residency constraints for EU customers so some traffic must stay in eu-west if possible
[00:53] Maya Chen: understood. high level architecture we typically recommend is policy router in front that uses prefer-local (latency bias) with capacity thresholds and a cost-fallback when regional capacity exhausted
[01:05] Emma Torres: by prefer-local you mean sticky affinity for sessions? we have session tokens tied to a user session across payment flows
[01:10] Luis Ortega: right — session affinity helps KV cache hits and reduces cold-starts. we do sticky routing with TTL aligned to KV cache TTLs so affinity doesn't cause long skew
[01:19] Ravi Menon: how do you prevent data from leaving region for EU-only customers — can policy pin to region even if capacity is low?
[01:26] Priya Kapoor: yes you can enforce hard residency rules — we support hard pinning to a region for certain customer segments. fallback is explicit: if pinned and no capacity, we either queue requests or failover to a compliant private deployment (e.g., on-prem cluster) depending on customer policy
[01:38] Samir Patel: queueing is tricky for payments, we prefer graceful degrade with retry and circuit-breaker not queueing long waits
[01:44] Luis Ortega: that's a sensible default. policy engine supports routing modes: latency-priority, cost-priority, and strict-residency. you can set region capacity threshold e.g. 80% nodes used to trigger spillover
[01:55] Julia Nguyen: can you explain spillover behavior? is it per-model, per-tenant?
[01:59] Luis Ortega: configurable at route or model level. common pattern: model-level routing where higher-accuracy model pinned to regional pool while a quantized variant in a fallback region handles overflow. the router can also route by tenant ID so you can keep enterprise customers on dedicated pools
[02:14] Maya Chen: important note — quantized fallbacks typically save 2–3x cost and improve throughput but you will see some quality delta, our Optimize tool recommends which prompts are sensitive
[02:24] Julia Nguyen: how do you validate quality on fallback? we want automated regression detection before failing over customer traffic
[02:29] Priya Kapoor: best practice is run canary shadow traffic to quantized variant and evaluate with your prompt set; Redwood supports production-esque eval harness and can compute BLEU/semantic similarity and threshold alarms
[02:40] Emma Torres: ok, about KV cache priming — what do you recommend for multi-region cold starts? our biggest pain is KV cache misses when routing goes to new region during failover
[02:48] Luis Ortega: two things — warmstart and pre-warm replication. warmstart: prefetch top N prefixes from hot requests into KV cache during deployment or when you detect impending surge. pre-warm replication: replicate hot keys to secondary regions asynchronously ahead of failover windows
[03:03] Samir Patel: does that replicate user-specific session keys? we have PII concerns
[03:07] Priya Kapoor: you control replication policy. sensitive keys can be excluded; only store tokenized or derivative keys that are privacy-preserving. for strict residency we'd avoid cross-region replication entirely and use on-prem private node as the failover target
[03:20] Ravi Menon: KMS and encryption — how are keys handled when replicating across regions? we need to show auditors
[03:25] Maya Chen: KMS is integrated, customer keys stay in their cloud KMS or HSM. we can configure regional key policies so cross-region decrypt is blocked. we'll include the KMS integration note in the security docs
[03:36] Julia Nguyen: latency-wise, what's the p95 impact when you hit a cold region with empty KV cache?
[03:41] Luis Ortega: cold region without KV: p95 can increase 2x-5x depending on model and sequence length. that's why we recommend warmstart and smaller batch windows to keep tail low. also continuous batching helps — small continuous batches minimize overhead compared to single-token calls
[03:58] Emma Torres: can you be more concrete with numbers? example: our ci-run prompt set average tokens 120 and concurrency 200 — what would we expect?
[04:08] Luis Ortega: rough baseline on an A100-like node: non-quantized model p95 ~140ms under steady state; cold region might jump to 350–600ms depending on KV miss rate. quantized variant p95 might be 90–200ms but with quality delta. we'll run a tailored benchmark for your prompt set to get exact figures
[04:26] Samir Patel: ok that helps. what about autoscaling delays? nodes spin up slower across clouds sometimes
[04:31] Maya Chen: Redwood Dedicated supports prewarmed spare nodes and burst capacity. for private/VPC we recommend a small warm reserve and node lifecycle scripts that keep a minimal pool always ready. autoscaler triggers at 60–70% utilization with predictive scaling for known scheduled jobs
[04:45] Julia Nguyen: predictive scaling — how do you feed in batch job schedules? we have daily reconciliation jobs that are big
[04:50] Priya Kapoor: you can schedule scaling windows and set surge capacity for scheduled jobs; also we'll let you submit a timeline API so the router can pre-provision nodes in the target region
[04:59] Emma Torres: runbook and DR playbook — can you show a short flow for regional outage?
[05:03] Luis Ortega: sure. step 1: detection — health probes failing to p95/availability thresholds. step 2: reduce new session affinity to allow in-flight to complete while blocking new sticky binds. step 3: enable spillover rule to secondary region with KV pre-warm + quantized fallback on for overflow. step 4: monitor quality/regressions, if threshold exceeded then enable circuit breaker and route to private dedicated pool or queue with customer-specific policy. step 5: post-incident reconciliation and cache rehydration back to primary region
[05:32] Samir Patel: what about order of operations for payments to avoid double-charge when failing over in mid-transaction?
[05:38] Maya Chen: recommended: use idempotency keys at application layer, and our router preserves request identifiers. for long lived transactions consider locking at platform level before cross-region failover; we can help design that pattern with your team
[05:48] Ravi Menon: auditor question: we need full traceability: which region served which token and evidence that we didn't move raw PII — can Redwood provide per-request trace and audit log?
[05:57] Priya Kapoor: yes, per-request tracing is available in Console. logs include region, model variant, node id, latency, and redacted request signatures. raw payloads are not stored unless you enable request retention and consent to storage for debugging
[06:11] Julia Nguyen: about batch sizing — how does batch size impact tail latency and KV cache behavior?
[06:16] Luis Ortega: larger batch sizes increase throughput but can add scheduling latency. continuous batching with dynamic windows is a good compromise: small time slices (e.g., 10–30ms) aggregate requests. for KV-aware batching, grouping by session or prefix improves cache hit and reduces kernel churn
[06:31] Emma Torres: and quantization? which quantization strategies do you support and do they change runtime memory profile?
[06:36] Luis Ortega: we support 8-bit LLM quantization, Q4 variants for certain architectures, and operator fusion kernels. quantized models reduce memory footprint and increase throughput but may change hallucination characteristics. we recommend per-prompt quality evaluations and incremental rollouts
[06:48] Samir Patel: we care about reproducibility of outputs if we switch models for failover — can Redwood pin seeds or force deterministic kernels?
[06:53] Priya Kapoor: absolute determinism is hard across different model variants and quantization, but for regression testing we provide stable inference environments and the ability to run shadow comparisons. we can expose random seeds but behavior may still vary slightly
[07:05] Julia Nguyen: about private deployments — if we wanted to run an on-prem fallback cluster, what are the network/connectivity requirements?
[07:11] Maya Chen: minimal: egress for control-plane reachability during install is required; for data path you can either fully isolate (no control plane egress) or use an interconnect/VPC peering. we have an offline install package for air-gapped customers but it takes more ops time
[07:25] Ravi Menon: and how do you handle model updates safely on private clusters? we need automated canary and rollback
[07:29] Luis Ortega: we publish model artifacts and image manifests. you can do blue/green or canary rollouts; Redwood console supports canary traffic split and automatic rollback on regression detection from your evals
[07:39] Emma Torres: okay realistic simulation — can you run a failover test that simulates us losing us-east for 3 minutes, traffic shifting to eu-west with sticky sessions and see KV miss rates and tail latency?
[07:49] Luis Ortega: yep that's exactly the plan for the benchmark. we'll do two runs: with and without pre-warm replication and with quantized fallback enabled. we'll surface per-route metrics and failure windows
[07:59] Samir Patel: for the benchmark, we'll provide a sample workload and keys, but we need to strip any PII. Julia will prepare that
[08:05] Julia Nguyen: yes will prepare PII-free set and upload to the shared folder you provide
[08:09] Maya Chen: perfect. quick note on runbook ops: we recommend a runbook page with playbook steps, run commands, and a checklist for safety: pre-warm, toggle routing rule, monitor, roll back. we'll share a template
[08:20] Ravi Menon: one more security thing: can we require SAML SSO and RBAC for runbook toggles? only two people should be able to flip the routing rule in prod
[08:28] Priya Kapoor: yes RBAC and SSO are supported. audit trail of who toggled values is recorded. we can lock toggles behind an approval flow or webhook to your ticketing system
[08:38] Maya Chen: okay i'm going to summarize the deliverables: policy doc + DR playbook template, benchmark run and spreadsheet, security artifacts and KMS notes, and schedule an on-prem walkthrough. anything else?
[08:49] Samir Patel: please include a sample quantized vs full-model quality report so our fraud team can evaluate false positives risk
[08:56] Luis Ortega: will do, we'll include quality delta per prompt class and recommended thresholds
[08:59] Emma Torres: thanks, that addresses most of our concerns
[09:02] Maya Chen: cool — we'll follow up with calendar invites. thanks everyone
[09:05] Julia Nguyen: thanks all
[09:06] End of transcript
